# Madrid Marks Five Years Since Deadly Train Bombings That Killed 191

**MADRID, Spain** — Survivors, victims' families, and government officials gathered at Madrid's Atocha train station Sunday to mark the fifth anniversary of the coordinated bombings that tore through the Spanish capital's commuter rail system, killing 191 people and wounding more than 1,800 others in the deadliest terrorist attack in modern Spanish history.

The ceremony, held at a memorial monument constructed at Atocha station, included a minute of silence at 7:39 a.m. — the exact time the first of ten bombs detonated on March 11, 2004, during the height of the morning rush hour.

King Juan Carlos, Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero, and opposition leaders set aside political differences to lay wreaths alongside relatives of victims, many of whom wept openly as the names of the dead were read aloud.

"Every year it feels the same as the first day," said Pilar Manjon, president of an association representing victims' families, whose own son was killed in the attacks. "The pain does not disappear. It only changes shape."

## A Coordinated Attack on the Morning Commute

The 2004 bombings targeted four commuter trains packed with passengers traveling into Madrid during the morning rush. Explosive devices, hidden in sports bags and backpacks, detonated almost simultaneously on trains at or near the Atocha, El Pozo, and Santa Eugenia stations.

Investigators later determined that Islamist extremists with loose ties to al Qaeda had planted the bombs, using mobile phones as detonators. The attacks came just three days before Spain's general election, a timing that many believe was designed to influence the political outcome and punish the country for its military involvement in Iraq.

The bombings triggered a massive manhunt that culminated weeks later in a dramatic standoff in the Madrid suburb of Leganes, where several suspects blew themselves up as police closed in, killing an elite police officer.

## Commuters Reflect on a City Forever Changed

For many Madrid residents who ride the same rail lines every day, the anniversary is a somber reminder of how ordinary life was violently interrupted.

"I take this train every morning, and I still think about it," said Carlos Fuentes, 34, an office worker who was on a different train that day but lost a coworker in the bombings. "You get on, you're thinking about work, about coffee, about nothing important — and for those people, that was the end."

Maria Delgado, who was 22 at the time and injured in the blast near El Pozo station, said she has only recently been able to ride trains without feeling a wave of anxiety.

"For a long time I couldn't do it," Delgado said. "Now I ride the trains again, but there's always a moment, especially in March, when I remember exactly where I was standing."

Younger commuters, many of whom were children in 2004, said the attacks remain a defining moment for their generation, similar to how older Americans speak of Sept. 11.

"My parents talk about that morning constantly," said university student Javier Ortiz, 19. "It's part of how this city understands itself now — before and after."

## A Legacy of Vigilance

In the years since the bombings, Spain has significantly overhauled its counterterrorism and intelligence operations, increasing cooperation with European security services and installing expanded surveillance systems throughout its rail network.

Officials say dozens of suspects have been convicted in connection with the attacks, though victims' relatives have long expressed frustration that some individuals believed to have played a role were acquitted or received what they consider lenient sentences.

Prime Minister Zapatero, addressing the crowd at Sunday's ceremony, said the anniversary was a moment to honor both the victims and the resilience of a city that refused to be broken.

"They wanted to divide us, to terrorize us, to change who we are," Zapatero said. "Instead, Madrid stood up the next day and kept moving forward, together."

As the ceremony concluded, station announcements resumed and commuters returned to the platforms, boarding trains for another ordinary Monday morning — a routine that, for this city, now carries the weight of memory.

**MADRID** — The morning light filtered gently through Atocha station this week as commuters paused, if only for a moment, near the memorial that has become a permanent fixture of the terminal—a glass cylinder etched with messages of grief and defiance. Nearly two decades after bombs tore through four commuter trains during the morning rush hour, killing 191 people and wounding nearly 2,000, the anniversary continues to summon a particular kind of stillness across this city.

Wreaths appeared at the station entrance before dawn. Elderly women in dark coats stood quietly, some crossing themselves, others simply staring at the wall of names. A single bell tolled 191 times, once for each life lost, echoing faintly against the marble.

"Every year it comes back," said Mercedes Ruiz, 58, who lost her nephew in the attack and has returned to Atocha every March 11th since. "People say time heals, but time only teaches you how to carry it differently. Some years I can barely walk through these doors. Other years, I need to."

For younger Madrileños, many of whom were children or not yet born when the bombs exploded, the day carries a different weight—inherited rather than lived.

"My mother tells me where she was standing when she heard the news," said Diego Martín, a 24-year-old university student. "I didn't experience it, but I feel like the city never fully let go of that morning. You can sense it in how quiet people get around this time of year."

## A Verdict That Left Questions Unanswered

The 2007 trial, which resulted in convictions for several individuals tied to the Islamist cell responsible for the bombings, remains a subject of quiet but persistent debate. Three men received lengthy sentences for their roles in planning and executing the attack, while several others were acquitted—verdicts that, for some victims' families, never fully closed the wound.

"The court gave us a version of justice," said Antonio Delgado, whose wife survived the bombing with lasting injuries. "But justice and peace are not always the same thing. We got names, sentences, prison walls. We didn't get her mornings back, the ones she still struggles through even now."

Legal experts have noted that the trial—one of the most complex in modern Spanish history—faced criticism for lingering ambiguities, including debates over the full scope of the network involved and whether all responsible parties were ever identified. That unfinished quality, many say, is part of why the anniversary still stings in a way that feels unresolved.

## A City That Remembers Together

Despite the sorrow, there is also, unmistakably, a thread of resilience running through the day. Local officials laid flowers at El Retiro Park, where a forest of cypress trees honors each victim individually. Choirs sang softly near the memorial forest. Strangers embraced.

"What I remember most isn't the fear," said Carmen Iglesias, a shop owner near Atocha who witnessed the aftermath firsthand in 2004. "It's how the whole city showed up for each other that day and every day after. That's what I choose to hold onto."

As the sun set over Madrid, the glass memorial at Atocha glowed faintly from within, its walls lined with handwritten notes left throughout the day—declarations of love, of loss, and, in many cases, of a stubborn, aching hope that such a morning never repeats itself.

For a city that has learned to carry grief alongside ordinary life, March 11th remains what it has always been: a day suspended between mourning and resolve, between memory and the quiet insistence on moving forward.

# Madrid Remembers: Five Years After the Train Bombings That Shook Spain

**MADRID** — On the morning of March 11, 2004, Manuela Torres boarded a commuter train at Alcalá de Henares station, just as she had every workday for the past six years. She doesn't remember the explosion that tore through her carriage. She remembers waking up on the platform, ears ringing, surrounded by twisted metal and silence that would soon give way to screams.

Five years later, Torres still takes the train to work. It's a choice, she says, "to not let them win."

## A Coordinated Assault on the Morning Commute

At the height of Madrid's morning rush hour, ten bombs concealed in sports bags detonated aboard four commuter trains traveling into the capital's Atocha station. The attacks, which unfolded between 7:37 and 7:40 a.m., struck trains at Atocha, El Pozo del Tío Raimundo, and Santa Eugenia stations.

The devices, hidden amid ordinary backpacks and gym bags, were packed with dynamite and detonated using mobile phones—a method that would later help investigators trace the plot back to a cell inspired by al-Qaeda, though not directly commanded by it. Spanish investigators determined the attack was carried out primarily by a group of Moroccan and Algerian nationals, some with loose affiliations to jihadist networks operating in Europe.

The death toll was staggering: 191 people killed, and more than 1,800 injured, making it the deadliest terrorist attack in Spanish history and the deadliest in Europe since the Lockerbie bombing in 1988.

## A Nation in Shock, A City Transformed

In the hours after the bombings, Madrid's emergency services were overwhelmed. Hospitals across the city opened their doors to a flood of wounded. Ordinary citizens lined up for blocks to donate blood. The Spanish Red Cross later called the response one of the largest civilian mobilizations in the country's modern history.

The political aftermath was almost as seismic as the attack itself. Initial government statements pointed toward the Basque separatist group ETA, a claim that was met with public skepticism and later proven false. The revelation that the attacks were linked to Islamist extremism—and accusations that the government had misled the public for political reasons ahead of national elections just three days later—triggered mass protests and contributed to the ruling party's stunning defeat at the polls.

## The Long Shadow of Trauma

Five years on, CNN spoke with survivors, victims' families, and mental health professionals about the lingering psychological wounds carried by a city that largely returned to normal life on the surface.

"There is no timeline for grief like this," said Dr. Carmen Ibáñez, a psychologist who has treated dozens of survivors since 2004. "Many of the people I still see today were physically uninjured. But they carry an invisible wound. Anniversaries, train whistles, the smell of certain metals—these things can trigger reactions years later."

Pilar Manjón, whose 20-year-old son Daniel was killed in the attack on the train at El Pozo, became one of the most visible voices representing victims' families in the years that followed, pushing for accountability and eventually helping found the Association of Victims of March 11.

"We are still here," Manjón told CNN. "We will always be here, asking for the truth, demanding that these people are never forgotten as statistics."

## Commuters Carry On, Warily

For ordinary Madrileños, the anniversary each year brings a complicated mix of remembrance and resilience. At Atocha station, a memorial—a translucent cylinder inscribed with condolence messages left by mourners in the attack's aftermath—stands as a quiet reminder above the platforms where chaos once reigned.

"You don't forget, but you also can't stop living," said Javier Martín, 34, who commutes daily through Atocha. "Every year on this date, the trains feel a little quieter. People are more aware. But we get on. We have to."

Security has visibly changed since 2004. Spanish rail authorities implemented increased camera surveillance, periodic bag checks, and coordination protocols with national police that didn't exist prior to the bombings. Yet many commuters acknowledge that a system built for millions of daily riders can never be fully impervious to attack.

"You make peace with a certain amount of risk," said Torres. "That's what living in a modern city means now, after Madrid, after London, after so many places."

## A Legacy of Legal Reckoning

The judicial process that followed the bombings was lengthy and, for many families, unsatisfying. In 2007, a Spanish court convicted 21 people in connection with the attacks, though three key defendants believed to have logistical roles received acquittals that sparked outrage among victims' groups. Several suspected plot leaders had already died in an April 2004 apartment standoff with police in the Madrid suburb of Leganés, detonating explosives rather than surrendering.

For many survivors, the convictions offered only partial closure.

"Justice in a court is not the same as justice in your heart," Manjón said. "But we keep fighting for both."

## Remembering Without Forgetting

As Spain marks five years since the attacks, officials in Madrid held commemorative ceremonies this week at Atocha station and at El Pozo del Tío Raimundo, with King Juan Carlos and Queen Sofía joining Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero and victims' families in moments of silence.

For a city that endured the deadliest attack in its history, the anniversary remains both a solemn duty and, increasingly, a testament to endurance.

"Madrid didn't break," said Martín, standing near the memorial at Atocha before catching his train. "It hurt, and it still hurts. But we're still here. Every single one of us who gets on that train each morning—we're proof of that."
